prize_parts.citation: for developing empirical methods to estimate demand, market power and competition in differentiated-product industries

statement.case_for: Random-coefficients discrete-choice demand estimation that handles endogenous prices (Berry 1994; Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes 1995) made it possible to measure substitution patterns, markups and welfare from market-level data. The approach is now routine in merger review, antitrust and regulation. It also spread to trade, health, environmental and public economics, so the reach goes well beyond industrial organisation. The work is about three decades old and has been tested through heavy use by academics, regulators and industry. Its limits are also well documented, including sensitivity to instruments, functional form and optimisation. Maturity and attribution of the demand-estimation core are therefore as clear as in any candidate on the list. After reading the colleagues' openings, I still think this is the strongest combination of conceptual change, methodological reach and policy use. I recognise that the committee's other leading candidates (B036, B034) have much broader opening support. I treat that support as information about how colleagues weigh fields, not as evidence about scientific merit.
statement.case_against: This is primarily a methodological toolkit rather than a single substantive discovery. The committee may prefer prizes for discoveries about how the economy works. Attribution is also genuinely awkward. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin have real claims, and Pakes' dynamic-oligopoly work (Ericson-Pakes) is not captured by a demand-estimation citation centred on Berry and Levinsohn. Structural estimates depend on modelling assumptions that are hard to verify, and the work is less aligned with the design-based empirical tradition recognised in 2021. Opening support is also thin: only four members ranked it, and only two placed it in their top three. If the committee judged it narrower or less broadly valued than the labour or trade candidates, B034 or B036 would be a reasonable choice.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks the BLP-and-dynamic-oligopoly candidate second, but asks whether Bresnahan or Reiss should displace Levinsohn or be added on priority. He also questions its fit with the committee's recent emphasis on design-based empirical work.
responses.response: The priority question is the right one, and I do not think it has a clean answer. Bresnahan's early empirical-IO and market-power work and Reiss's entry models pre-date BLP and shaped the field. The citation I propose is narrower, however: demand estimation with endogenous prices and heterogeneous consumers. On that formulation Berry and Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes are the defining contributions, and Levinsohn's role in the 1995 paper and the applications is direct. I would not defend the trio as the only defensible choice. If the committee wants a broader empirical-IO citation, Bresnahan would belong and the trio would have to change. On the design-based point, I would not treat the 2021 prize as setting the committee's preferred method. Structural methods answer counterfactual questions such as mergers and entry that reduced-form designs cannot address. That is a complement, not a substitute.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks the demand-estimation candidate fourth. He sees the committee choosing between the demand-estimation core and the dynamic-games line, notes that Bresnahan's claim may be seen as equal, and observes that structural assumptions are often hard to verify.
responses.response: I agree that the demand-versus-dynamics choice is the central attribution question, and the three-name cap makes it hard. I resolve it in favour of the demand-estimation core because that is where adoption and practical use are most pervasive, and where the identification logic is clearest. Pakes is the one name who spans both strands, which gives the trio some coverage of the dynamic literature without crediting it in the citation. On unverifiable assumptions, I concede the point. Structural demand estimates can be sensitive to instruments and functional form. That is a limit on how much to trust any one estimate, not on whether the method changed how market power and welfare are measured. The same transparency concern applies to the quantitative trade models behind B034, so I do not think it separates the candidates.

responses.point: Enflo ranks firm heterogeneity and trade first. She takes Melitz (2003) as the central contribution with Helpman as the lineage, treats Redding as later and more derivative, and notes that Krugman's 2008 prize already covers part of the territory.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing case from my own broad field, and I rank it second. I agree with the attribution to Melitz and Helpman, and I agree that Redding's quantitative work is better left out of a two-person core. I am less comfortable treating Krugman's 2008 prize as a minor overlap. The Melitz model is a real conceptual advance, but it sits within the monopolistic-competition framework Krugman was recognised for, and priority questions with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum remain. I therefore keep it as my first alternative rather than my preferred award. This is a close call, and I would not oppose a B034 prize on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Hassler ranks the China-shock and technology candidate second. He sees Autor, Dorn and Hanson as the natural trio for the trade-shock work, observes that the ballot item merges two related literatures, and notes that the framing of the prize motivation could therefore vary.
responses.response: The merging of the two literatures is my main reservation about B036 and the reason I rank it only seventh. The task-based framework and the China-shock evidence have different originators, and Acemoglu's earlier recognition complicates the task side. A prize built on Autor, Hanson and Dorn would rest on the trade-shock evidence, whose magnitudes and persistence are still debated. I accept that the work has had large effects on research and policy and that it has had a decade of replication. I would not oppose it, and I name it as an alternative. I do not see it as clearly stronger than B020 once the dispute over long-run magnitudes and the technology/trade split is taken into account.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would credit only the demand-estimation core, or a broader empirical-IO prize that includes Bresnahan or the dynamic-industry strand, which would change the trio.
Whether the committee values a methods contribution with very broad use as equal to a substantive discovery, given the thin opening support for this candidate.
How the committee would weigh the 2008 trade prize and the priority questions with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum when comparing B034 with B020.
My assessment relies on my own knowledge of the literature and has not been independently verified, and my field proximity may bias me upward.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the credited names on this shortlist is apparent from the supplied profile. The profile lists co-authorship with committee colleagues John Hassler and Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026) on a topic unrelated to these candidates. It also lists research in industrial organisation and international pricing, which is adjacent to B020 and B034. The profile's public note on his spouse's political role has no apparent bearing on any shortlisted candidate.
